units.blurb: Follows human origins and migration out of Africa, then the Neolithic Revolution and the tradeoffs that came with farming and settled life.

lessons.title: Human Origins, Evolution, and Why Humans Survived
lessons.overview: From a 3-million-year-old skeleton with no words, what can we honestly PROVE about our earliest ancestors, and where exactly does the evidence run out?

lessons.title: Migration Out of Africa and the Geography of Survival
lessons.overview: If every human alive descends from Africa, how do fossils AND genes let us reconstruct the ORDER in which our ancestors filled the Earth?

lessons.title: Paleolithic Life: Tools, Fire, Cave Art, Kinship, and Risk
lessons.overview: Bones and tools prove early humans survived, but what does a painted bull or a carved figure prove that bones never could?

lessons.title: Forager Society Simulation
lessons.overview: Foragers had no farms, no houses, and no stores, so when the season turned against them, what kept the band alive, and why was MOVING the answer for 90% of human history?

lessons.title: The Neolithic Revolution as a Turning Point
lessons.overview: When humans started farming, what chain of changes did one choice set off, and was settling down our greatest step forward or, as Jared Diamond says, “the worst mistake” we ever made?

lessons.title: Farming, Domestication, Surplus
lessons.overview: Once a village grew MORE food than it could eat, who decided where the extra went, and how did that single question create the first rich, the first powerful, and the first rulers?

lessons.title: Tradeoffs of Farming
lessons.overview: Skeletons keep the receipts. Using measured evidence, height, dental disease, anemia, and life expectancy, did the Neolithic Revolution make the average person BETTER off or WORSE off, and if it was so bad, why did farming still spread to every continent?

sources.text: It is reported that, returning from his final pilgrimage, the Prophet Muhammad stopped at a place called Ghadir Khumm and addressed the Muslims gathered with him. He first asked them: “Do I not have more right over the believers than they have over themselves?” The people answered, “Yes.” He then took the hand of his cousin and son-in-law Ali and said: “He whose mawla I am, Ali is his mawla.”
sources.credit: — The hadith (reported saying) of Ghadir Khumm, recorded in Sunni collections such as the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the works of al-Tirmidhi, and central to Shia tradition. lessons.title: Worlds Around 1400 to Muslim, Christian, and Neo-Confucian Realms
lessons.overview: Standing in the year 1400, which civilization would you have BET on to rule the next 500 years, and why did the realm with the best assets NOT launch global expansion, while fragmented Europe eventually did?

sources.text: “I set out alone, having neither fellow-traveller in whose companionship I might find cheer, nor caravan whose party I might join, but swayed by an overmastering impulse within me and a desire long-cherished in my bosom to visit these illustrious sanctuaries [Mecca and Medina]. lessons.title: Italian Renaissance, Humanism and City-States
lessons.overview: The Italian Renaissance ran on three ingredients, WEALTH, RECOVERED IDEAS, and INDIVIDUALS. If you could remove only ONE, which removal would do the most damage, and what does that tell you about why it began in Italy?

lessons.title: Northern Renaissance and the Printing Press
lessons.overview: Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1450) did not just make books, it MULTIPLIED every idea it touched. Trace the cascade outward (1st → 2nd → 3rd order) and decide which downstream effect would most reshape the next 100 years.

lessons.title: Martin Luther and the Protestant Reformation Begins
lessons.overview: Luther's Ninety-Five Theses were a list of COMPLAINTS. Sort each one, was it about MONEY, POWER, or BELIEF?, and decide which KIND of grievance was most dangerous to the Church, and why this protest spread when earlier ones were silenced.

lessons.title: Protestant Reformation Spreads, Calvin and Henry VIII
lessons.overview: The Reformation spread for very different REASONS. Diagnose three break-from-Rome movements on a THEOLOGY ←→ POLITICS spectrum, and test whether a reform's MOTIVE predicts how its new church was governed.

lessons.title: Catholic Counter-Reformation and Wars of Religion
lessons.overview: The Catholic Church did TWO opposite things at once: it REFORMED itself and it fought BACK. Sort its Counter-Reformation measures into reform vs. reaction, and judge whether the response was mostly self-correction or self-defense, and whether it worked.

units.title: Age of Exploration Encounter and Exchange
units.blurb: Follows the Age of Exploration, conquest in the Americas, the Columbian Exchange, the Atlantic slave trade, and the rise of mercantile companies.

lessons.title: Why Europeans Crossed Oceans, Causes of Exploration
lessons.overview: Why did Europeans who would not sail out of sight of land in 1450 cross whole oceans by 1500 to was it desire, fear, or new tools?

lessons.title: Portuguese Exploration, Henry the Navigator and Vasco da Gama
lessons.overview: How did Portugal, small, poor, and on the edge of Europe, build the first sea route to Asia: was it one leader, or a STACK of innovations no one of which works alone?

lessons.title: Spanish Exploration, Columbus and the Americas
lessons.overview: Why did Columbus change world history while remaining completely wrong about what he had done, and how did what he ASSUMED about the people he met shape everything that followed?

lessons.title: Conquest of the Americas, Cortés, Pizarro, and Encomienda
lessons.overview: How did a few hundred Spaniards defeat empires of millions, was it European 'superiority,' or a combination of disease, alliances, and circumstance that the Indigenous record reveals?

lessons.title: The Columbian Exchange, Plants, Animals, Diseases, People
lessons.overview: After 1492, what living things crossed the ocean between the hemispheres, and why did the same exchange that fed Europe's growth also help cause catastrophe in the Americas?

lessons.title: Disease and the Collapse of Indigenous Populations
lessons.overview: How did Old World disease kill an estimated 80 to 95% of the Indigenous people of the Americas, how do we know, and how should we classify what happened?

lessons.title: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade, Origins and Scale
lessons.overview: Why did European demand for plantation labor drive the trans-Atlantic slave trade, and how do we hold its scale (about 12.5 million people) and its human cost together, so that neither the numbers nor the people disappear?

About 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage; roughly 15% — close to 2 million people — died during the crossing itself.
